doc.title: Dan Barrett interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995

title: Ken Owen steers him from trumpet to trombone
summary: In fifth grade the band teacher Ken Owen, judging his embouchure, suggests trombone over the trumpet he wanted; Barrett later suspects Owen needed trombonists.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the horn: first instrument and the trombone

blocks.x: Marvelous. What led you to start playing the trombone other than any other instrument?

Well, actually I wanted to play trumpet, and in fifth grade I remember very clearly a gentleman came in and our teacher introduced him and she said his name was Ken Owen, and he taught in the band at our local junior high school. And many of us would be graduating from the elementary school and going on to his junior high school. And he told us he had a concert band over at the junior high and that he was starting a beginning band program at the elementary school for fifth and sixth graders. And he made a little speech, parts of which I still remember. I was about eleven years old, and he told us, or I guess you could say he reminded us that music is kind of a part of our daily lives,

whether we play music or not, that we’re continually surrounded by music and he said many of you have parents who will play the radio when you’re in the car and if you go shopping you hear music in the supermarket, and if you go to the dentist’s office they usually have music playing. And he said of course there’s background music for television shows. So he pointed out how big a part music plays in our everyday lives, and he said that he knew that some of us were probably thinking that we would like to try and make music ourselves instead of just listen to it, maybe some of us would like to try to play music ourselves. So he asked us to go home and talk it over with our parents, and he asked us to think about at least three instruments, three different instruments that we might want to play, because he thought that we might be more suited toward one instrument than the other. So the following week I came back. Mr. Owen led a bunch of us out of the class, so that was kind of exciting, we got out of the fifth grade class you know, to walk down to the auditorium. And he had several real instruments there and then to represent the instruments that he didn’t have physically there he had pictures. So he brought pictures of French horns and violas and that kind of thing. And he asked us to sit by the picture of our first choice of instrument. So I went over and sat near a trumpet, because that’s what I wanted to play. And he introduced himself to me and I told him my name and he kind of looked over my, they call it the embouchure, the lip muscles or chops we call them, and he said, “well gee, Danny, I don’t know about playing trumpet. I think with your embouchure and the way your teeth are formed, you’d probably be better off playing the trombone.” And I still have a healthy respect for Mr. Owen, but I found out a couple of years later, he had all the trumpet players he needed in the junior high band, and he didn’t have any trombone players coming in. So he thought he’d cultivate a trombone player you see? And I finally got to seventh grade, I joined his band. He had about 15 trumpet players and three trombone players. And you know in the concert band, it’s always the trumpets and sometimes the clarinets, but generally the trumpets that play the melodies to the songs. And what do the trombones do? They play the long whole notes in the background, making those guys sound good. You know what I mean. And after a couple of months of that, I told Mr. Owen I said, “I don’t want to play these long boring notes, I want to play the melody. That’s why I wanted to play music. So I want to play the trumpet.” And he said, “well you know, Danny, he said, you can play the melody on trombone.” I said, “no, no, no you can’t.” Because I didn’t think you could. I’d never heard that done. And he said, “ask your parents if you can come in tomorrow morning early.” I think class was at 8:00. He said, “come in at 7:30 and I’ll play you some records of trombone players playing the melody.” So I showed up at 7:30 and I’m sure Hamilton College is far better equipped than our junior high school, but do you remember those big old fashioned phonographs — the 33, 45 and 78?
